Management Decision Support Tools for Cambridge Bay Arctic Char

Tom Carruthers tom@bluematterscience.com

02 February, 2026

 

 

1 Disclaimer

The following work is preliminary and intended only as tool for eliciting feedback on data, modelling and other aspects of this fishery.

None of these results are final.

These analyses do not necessarily reflect the point of view of DFO and in no way anticipate DFO future policy.

2 Objectives

Develop an decision support tool for guiding data collection, scientific assessment and management advice for Cambridge Bay Arctic Char.

There are various components to this work:

  • Determine a suitable modeling framework for resolving ref points for Cambridge Bay Arctic Char,

  • Determine appropriate data collection protocols (scientific - to improve assessments, management - to support management decision making that can achieve objectives).

  • Extending/incorporating that model for exploratory fisheries and developing a data collection framework that will potentially inform assessments of the fisheries (e.g., how many years of data, frequency of data collection, what type of data are the priorities, etc.),

  • Start exploring frameworks for incorporating environmental and mixed-stock fishery data.

9 Fitted Operating Models

An example of a prelminary statistical catch-at-age model (RCM, Huynh 2024) fit for the Ekalluk river is available here which provides a summary of diagnostics available.

The aim is to synthesize the available data for each river and conduct similar fits for assumptions that span a plausible range of uncertainties.

These operating models can be used to design data collection and management procedures.

10 The ArcticChar R Package

10.1 Functionality

The aim of the R package is to provide a single source for objects (data inputs, fitted operating models) and code (management options, custom figures) used in the provision of management advice. These are intended to be public-facing and pubically available in support of peer review. By building the package from a GitHub repository progress and features can be tracked and version control can be implemented.

10.2 Installation

The Arctic Char R package uses the openMSE libraries for fitting operating models and conducting simulation tests. To install openMSE:

install.packages('openMSE')

Using the remotes package, the latest version of the ArcticChar R package can be installed driectly from the GitHub repo:

library(remotes)
install_github('Blue-Matter/ArcticChar')

You can check package versions using:

packageVersion('openMSE')
packageVersion('ArcticChar')

10.3 Objects

In this preliminary version, ArcticChar only includes a small number of demonstration objects. One of those is the RCM fitting object for Ekalluk River and the resulting operating model. You can find those using the avail function:

library(ArcticChar)
avail('RCModel') # the available RCM fitted models
avail('OM')      # the operating model resulting from those fits

class?OM         # help documentation about operating models
class?RCModel    # help documentation on RCM model fit objects

10.4 Origins of RCMfit

The Fit_Ekalluk object is the output of the RCM fitting function. That output actually includes the two principle inputs to the fitting process:

  • An OM object without any of the fitted estimates - recruitment, fishing mortality rates, selectivity).
  • A formatted data object of class RCMdata

You can use these to redo the model fitting. Perhaps you want to change some of the fitting options such as likelihood functions or data weighting, or maybe just out of curiousity to see it in action.

To do that, remove the OM and RCMdata objects from the RCMfit output and rerun RCM:

OM = Fit_Ekalluk@OM                          # The input OM object
RCMdata = Fit_Ekalluk@data                   # The RCM data object

setup()                                      # Set up parallel computation
fit = RCM(OM,                                # Blank operating model object missing Rec, F and sel estimates
          RCMdata,                           # Formatted RCMdata object
          s_selectivity='logistic_length',   # Survey selectivity is parameterized as logistic and length based
          mean_fit = T,                      # Include a single model fit at the mean value of the various input parameters
          drop_nonconv=T,                    # Drop any simulations (draws of parameters) that led to non-convergence
          drop_highF=T,                      # Drop any simulations (draws of parameters) that hit F max bounds
          cores=8)                           # Do the calculations in parallel over 8 threads


?RCM                                         # Find out more about the Rapid Conditioning Model

10.5 Examining input data

library(ArcticChar)
data = Fit_Ekalluk@data        # Take the input data from the fitted RCM model
class(data)                    # What class is is this
## [1] "RCMdata"
## attr(,"package")
## [1] "SAMtool"
class?RCMdata                  # Find out more about how data is formatted for RCM
## starting httpd help server ... done
yearlabel = data@Misc$CurrentYr - (data@Misc$nyears-1):0 # make the right year label
plot(yearlabel, data@Chist, xlab="Year", ylab = "Catches (kg)") # plot the catches

10.6 Plotting model fit

To generate an html report file for a fitted RCM object, you can use the generic plot method:

library(ArcticChar)
plot(Fit_Ekalluk)

The same works for the OM object:

plot(OM_Ekalluk)

10.7 Example closed-loop simulations

Operating models are used to test management options over projected years.

First start by reconstructing the historical fishery and calculate all management reference points using Simulate:

Hist = Simulate(OM_Ekalluk)
## ℹ slot Fdisc has only one value (0.5). Using this value for both lower and upper bounds.
## ℹ slot DR has only one value (0). Using this value for both lower and upper bounds.
## ℹ slot Ebiascv has two values, but only one required. Using first value (0).
## → Loading operating model
## 
## → Optimizing for user-specified movement
## 
## → Calculating MSY reference points for each year
## 
## → Calculating historical stock and fishing dynamics
## 
## → Calculating per-recruit reference points
## 
## → Calculating B-low reference points
## 
## → Calculating reference yield - best fixed F strategy
## 
## → Simulating observed data
## 
## → Updating Simulated Data with Real Data from `OM@cpars$Data`
## Warning in check_Index_Fit(Stats, i): An error occurred in calculating statistical properties of fit to Additional Index 1 (possibly because there was only one observed data point). 
## Using the index observation error for slot `Ind` from `Obs` object (or possibly conditioned if `cpars$Data@Ind` was provided).
## Use `cpars$AddIerr` to manually set the observation error.
?Simulate              # help documentation

Note this returns a warning abotu index 1 which is a placeholder and only has one observation - openMSE cannot calculate statistical properties of indices if the only have 1 observation!

You can now select a management option and do a projection:

The MSE object contains all the information about the projections such as catches, spawning biomass, recruitment etc. You can make your own plotting methods or just use the generic tools in openMSE such as the ‘simple plot’ Splot():

Splot(MSE)

class?MSE  # find out more about objects of class MSE

There are also some DFO-specific performance plots:

DFO_proj(MSE) # overfishing / underfishing at the end of the time series

?DFO_proj     # help documentation

Reference Point Calculator (Huynh et al. 2022) is an R package and App designed for the exploration of reference points and the testing of management procedures / Harvest Control Rules (HCRs). 10.9 Empirical Management Procedures

The OpenMSE framework was expressly designed to provide a fast and powerful environment for testing fishery management procedures (MPs). An MP is any reproducible rule for calculating management advice from data. This could be setting TACs as a multiplier of some recent index level (a so called ‘empirical MP’) or the use of a data-rich stock assessment and harvest control rule. MPs can also be tested with varying qualities of data allowing for the evaluation of data collection protocols (how often, how frequent, what variable).

For a demonstration we will design a constant exploitation rate management procedure of the type used in the management of high profile economically important species such as Atlantic Bluefin tuna.

Since we do not yet have an index of abundance (real data) from which to run the simulations (openMSE uses the historical data and generates projected data based on the statistical properties of RCM fit) we will use a generic index of abundance ‘Ind’ that is provided for every year of an openMSE forward projection. This index has statistical properties determined by slots in the operating model object. Its variance, phrased as a coefficient of variation is slot (Iobs). You can actually view the past and future error structure of this simulated index in the Hist object:

OM_Ekalluk@Iobs   # Two values (upper and lower bounds) on the biomass index CV
class?Obs         # These are properties of the Obs object (observation error model) that makes up part of the OM
Hist@SampPars$Obs$Ierr_y # The matrix (simulation by year) of index errors (phrased as mulitpliers)
plot(density(Hist@SampPars$Obs$Ierr_y)) # look at the distribution

You can view these simulated data in the Data slot of the historical reconstruction object Hist. From that you can work out roughly the current ratio of catch to index and set up an empirical rule that keeps this constant exploitation rate (Catch / Index) in future years.

Data = Hist@Data
Catches = Data@Cat
Index = Data@Ind
last5years = dim(Catches)[2] - 4:0
Catchlast5 = mean(Catches[,last5years])       # about 15000 kg
CI_ratio = Catchlast5 / sum(Index[, last5years]) # ratio is about 13000 kg / Index

MPs work for a simulation x and the same kind of Data object we used above. We are going to take the mean of the last three index observations and set a TAC that is based on the ratio calculated above. We will compare this to an MP that is a constant catch of catches from the last 5 years.

EMP = function(x, Data, reps=NA, ...){ # Empirical MP
  CI_ratio = 13000                    # recent historical ratio of catches: index
  nyears = dim(Data@Ind)[2]           # most recent three years of index data
  last_3 = nyears - 0:2               # the index for the last three years
  Rec = new('Rec')                    # make a new recommendation object class?Rec
  I_last_3 = mean(Data@Ind[x,last_3]) # mean of index over last three years
  Rec@TAC = I_last_3 * CI_ratio       # TAC recommendation is linearly related to population size
  Rec
}

CC = function(x, Data, reps = NA, ...){ # Constant catch
  Rec = new('Rec')
  Rec@TAC = 15000                     # Catch never changes, its 15000 kg for every projection year
  Rec
}

class(EMP) = class(CC) = "MP"     # Assign the functions the openMSE class 'MP'

You can now run a projection and compare results:

myProj = Project(Hist,c("CC","EMP"))
Splot(myProj)

In this example, recent catches were too high to be maintained and crashed the stock withing 15 years. The responsive index based MP responded to available biomass and keep the stock near BMSY levels.

Clearly much more advanced empirical MPs are possible that use a wide range of fishery inputs but the principle is well illustrated in this example.

17 Appendix

17.1 RCM

17.1.1 Overview

Arctic Char operating models were fitted using the age-structured Rapid Conditioning Model (RCM) in the SAMtool package (Huynh et al. 2025) included in the openMSE framework. The RCM is a statistical catch-at-age (or catch-at-length) model similar to stock assessment frameworks such as the Woods Hole Assessment Model (WHAM; Stock and Miller 2021) in that it is implemented in R using the Template Model Builder (TMB) library for non linear estimation (Kristensen et al. 2016). RCM has two important advantages over dedicated data-rich assessment packages that make it suited to conditioning operating models for the invertebrate case studies of this project: (1) it can accept a wide range of data types of varying sparsity, for example, catches by numbers for urchins and a combination of absolute biomass survey, age data and CPUE data for geoduck; (2) it is designed to fit to Monte Carlo samples of model parameters, conducting an individual model fit to, for example, a sample of steepness, natural mortality rate and somatic growth. In this application, the RCM can capture a much larger range of uncertainty in reconstructed fishing mortality and recruitment than a typical data-rich assessment model.

17.1.2 RCM Applications

The RCM has previously been applied as an operating model conditioning approach in various peer-reviewed applications such as evaluation of rebuilding strategies for B.C. Inside Yelloweye Rockfish (Haggarty et al. 2022), development of management procedures for B.C. Inside Quillback Rockfish (DFO 2023b), the Bay of Fundy Herring MSE (Carruthers et al., 2023a) and in support of the MERA approach to data-moderate fisheries management (Carruthers et al., 2023b). The RCM has also been used to demonstrate OM conditioning in preliminary MSE analyses for a range of pelagic species such as South Atlantic Swordfish (Taylor et al. 2022), North Atlantic Blue Shark (Carruthers 2024) and Pacific Neon Flying Squid (Dai 2025).
